definition: Prosaic means plain, ordinary, and lacking imagination.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word prosaic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know prosaic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: He christened the rowboat 'Rowboat,' explaining that after forty years as a patent clerk he preferred his afternoons prosaic.
Plain is honest simplicity and can even be a virtue — milder than prosaic, which begins to accuse the writing of having no imagination at all.
Humdrum goes further than prosaic: past unimaginative into the numbing drone of sameness, the same beige day repeating without end.

Pedestrian writing trudges along without lift or surprise — the complaint is about dullness. Prosaic overlaps, but it diagnoses the cause: language that stays literal and earthbound, refusing every chance at imagery. A pedestrian paragraph merely bores; a prosaic one may still inform you — it just never leaves the ground.

Unimaginative is the blunt complaint that no invention went in — no new idea, no fresh angle anywhere. Prosaic adds the texture of the result: flat, literal, everyday wording. An unimaginative plan lacks ideas; prosaic language can carry a decent idea and still plod, word by earthbound word.

By night, Teodoro Vasquez publishes poems full of weather and myth; by day, he writes instruction manuals for a dishwasher company.
Interviewers keep asking how he bears it, and he keeps correcting them.

Manual writing must be prosaic, he says, and he means it as a compliment: 'When the kitchen is flooding, nobody wants my metaphors.' In a manual, water is water, a hose is a hose, and every sentence walks the reader straight to the shutoff valve.
He saves his images for the poems, he says, and his readers — both kinds — are better off for the division.
